title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
summary: Worldwide Express automated its less-than-truckload freight billing-exception process with a multi-agent solution built on Amazon Bedrock. Six months after launch, the company cut active exceptions by 75%, improved time-to-cash by four weeks, and unlocked $10 million in free cash flow.
content:
Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.
Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.
In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.
The challenge
In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:

Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.

Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:

Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
Research the root cause in vendor records.
Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
Wait for a response.
Execute the resolution in the TMS.

With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.
Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.
From assessment to production
In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.
How it works
The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.
Agents
When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:

Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.

Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.
Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .
Actions
The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.
Carrier knowledge base
Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.
Human-in-the-loop
The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.
Observability
Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.
End-to-end flow
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.

Figure 1: Worldwide Express’s AI-powered exception handling architecture on AWS

Results
Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.
The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.

“With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”
— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express

Looking forward
Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.
Conclusion
Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.
To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock . Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
summary: The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). This post walks through a controlled local deployment that routes model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West) using API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions, so a security team can validate it before broader use.
content:
The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) , providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.
This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1 , where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.
Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.
For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.
This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.
Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.
Solution overview
You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:

Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.

The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1 . Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.
Walkthrough
The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.
Prerequisites
Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files.
Step 1: Set up authentication
Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1 . Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile codex-il5 . Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.
Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.
The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain . AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.
The app first checks for AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through %USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env on Windows or ~/.codex/.env on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.
If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials and related profile settings from ~/.aws/config . On Windows, the corresponding default paths are %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\config . The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation .
Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files
You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: config.toml and requirements.toml .
Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.

Operating system
User config.toml
Admin requirements.toml

Windows
%USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml
%ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml

Linux
~/.codex/config.toml
/etc/codex/requirements.toml

macOS
~/.codex/config.toml
/etc/codex/requirements.toml

Start from the requirements.toml file. requirements.toml is an administrator-controlled rules file. It sets security limits that users can’t override, for example, restricting which permission levels, tools, or settings the ChatGPT desktop app is allowed to use.
Use the following baseline for the supported AWS GovCloud (US) Amazon Bedrock deployment. The [windows] section applies only to Windows, and sandbox_private_desktop must be supported by the approved runtime.

allowed_login_methods = ["api"]
allowed_sandbox_modes = ["read-only", "workspace-write"]
allowed_approvals_reviewers = ["user"]
allowed_approval_policies = [
{ granular = { sandbox_approval = false, rules = true,
mcp_elicitations = false, request_permissions = false,
skill_approval = true } },
]
allowed_web_search_modes = ["disabled", "cached"]
allow_browser_and_computer_use = false
allow_appshots = false
allow_remote_control = false
allow_login_shell = false
allow_managed_hooks_only = true
check_for_update_on_startup = false
mcp_servers = {}

[feedback]
enabled = false

[features]
network_proxy = true
in_app_chat = false
in_app_dictation = false
in_app_browser = false
browser_use = false
browser_use_external = false
browser_use_full_cdp_access = false
computer_use = false
in_app_updates = false
image_generation = false
memories = false
chronicle = false
external_agent_memory_import = false
guardian_approval = false
guardianv2 = false
guardian_ext = false
apps = false
enable_mcp_apps = false
plugins = false
remote_plugin = false
plugin_sharing = false
recommended_plugins = false
skill_mcp_dependency_install = false
skill_search = false
workspace_dependencies = false
hooks = false
standalone_web_search = false

[experimental_network]
enabled = true
managed_allowed_domains_only = true
domains = {}
unix_sockets = {}
allow_upstream_proxy = false
dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy = false
dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets = false
allow_local_binding = false

[application.network]
enabled = true

[application.network.domains]
"bedrock-mantle.us-gov-west-1.api.aws" = "allow"
"api.openai.com" = "deny"
"chat.openai.com" = "deny"
"chatgpt.com" = "deny"
"ab.chatgpt.com" = "deny"
"platform.openai.com" = "deny"
"auth.openai.com" = "deny"
"gov.api.openai.com" = "deny"
"gov.chatgpt.com" = "deny"
"sdfedpreastus2.oaiusercontent.com" = "deny"
"o33249.ingest.us.sentry.io" = "deny"
"persistent.oaistatic.com" = "deny"
"oaisidekickupdates.blob.core.windows.net" = "deny"

[windows]
allowed_sandbox_implementations = ["elevated"]
sandbox_private_desktop = true

Next, configure the config.toml file. config.toml tells the ChatGPT desktop app how to operate, including which model provider to use ( amazon-bedrock ), which model to select, and settings such as permissions or context limits.
Replace the model ID and named profile (for example, codex-il5 ) with approved values.

model = "REPLACE_WITH_APPROVED_MODEL_ID"
model_provider = "amazon-bedrock"
forced_login_method = "api"
approval_policy = { granular = { sandbox_approval = false,
rules = true, mcp_elicitations = false,
request_permissions = false, skill_approval = true } }
approvals_reviewer = "user"
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
web_search = "cached"
allow_login_shell = false
check_for_update_on_startup = false

[model_providers.amazon-bedrock]
base_url = "https://bedrock-mantle.us-gov-west-1.api.aws/openai/v1"
wire_api = "responses"
requires_openai_auth = false
supports_websockets = false
supports_standalone_web_search = false

[model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws]
region = "us-gov-west-1"
profile = "codex-il5"

[sandbox_workspace_write]
network_access = false

[features]
network_proxy = true

[analytics]
enabled = false

[feedback]
enabled = false

[otel]
exporter = "none"
trace_exporter = "none"
metrics_exporter = "none"
log_user_prompt = false

[memories]
generate_memories = false
use_memories = false

[skills.bundled]
enabled = false

[apps._default]
enabled = false

[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"

Step 3: Launch, initialize, and verify
Download the app from the ChatGPT site and install it. Leave the app closed after installation. If it opens automatically or if the app has been launched previously, fully exit ChatGPT and end any lingering ChatGPT or Codex processes.
Make sure requirements.toml and config.toml are in place before the first app launch.
Start the app to load the requirements.toml and config.toml settings. Make sure it shows amazon-bedrock as the model provider.
In the Codex CLI, you should see a /status tab that looks like this:

Figure 1: The Codex CLI /status tab confirming amazon-bedrock as the model provider

In the ChatGPT desktop app, you can also confirm amazon-bedrock as the model provider.

Figure 2: The ChatGPT desktop app settings showing amazon-bedrock as the model provider

Troubleshooting
The application prompts for an OpenAI account. Verify that requirements.toml and config.toml use the exact locations and file names shown in the preceding table, terminate all ChatGPT and Codex processes, and relaunch. The files must precede app launch.
AWS GovCloud (US) endpoint is reported as unsupported. Confirm the exact desktop or app-server release, endpoint, and model with OpenAI. Changing the URL alone does not establish support.
The wrong AWS identity is used. Inspect the effective credential source and named profile. Check whether an Amazon Bedrock API key takes precedence over the profile.
Capability restrictions are missing. Inspect the full effective requirements after restart. The API-only sign-in setting doesn’t apply the capability policy.
Rollback and cleanup
If a validation check fails, stop the rollout. Return the affected devices to the previously approved policy and provider settings, then restart the ChatGPT desktop app. Revoke any temporary AWS credentials or API keys, and confirm that those devices can no longer connect to Amazon Bedrock. Keep a record of the test and clearly document what failed before trying again.
Conclusion
The ChatGPT desktop app on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) gives you a controlled way to use OpenAI frontier models and coding assistance. Inference stays in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. By validating the configuration, confirming the approved AWS identity and endpoint, and verifying security controls, you can confidently prepare the deployment for broader use. This approach supports innovation while aligning deployment decisions with each organization’s security, authorization, and data-handling requirements.
Ready to explore the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)? Start with a controlled deployment, validate your security controls, and work with your security team to prepare for broader adoption.

Virgil is a Senior Partner Solutions Architect at AWS and a GenAI and AI/ML specialist. He helps partners and customers integrate OpenAI technologies with AWS services, transforming innovative ideas into scalable, real-world business solutions.

title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
summary:
Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.
The post From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence appeared first on Microsoft Research .
content:
At a glance

Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.

To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.

The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.

Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.

Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.

Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence.

They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in.

We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars:

Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data

Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets

Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation

Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform

Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ?

In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot.

Synthetic enterprise environments

Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve.

Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.

Grounding in real world signals

To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources.

O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates.

Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions.

SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization.

Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation

Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure.

Industry specific simulation

We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage:

A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings

A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews

An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination

Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation

This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes.

Automated query generation

While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in.

The six-stage pipeline

Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries

We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios.

Validating synthetic quality

Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions:

Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships?

Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns?

Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics?

Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals?

End-to-end automation

While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including:

Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases.

Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand.

Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles.

Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels.

This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results.

Privacy and safety by design

Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk.

Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline.

This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible.

Results and impact

Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions.

On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments.

On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs.

On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure.

Conclusion

As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety.

Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next.

At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale .

Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets !

light_analysis.summary: 微软研究院推出“行业评估数据生成平台”，为Microsoft Copilot构建基于O*NET、招聘信息和SEC文件等公开数据的大规模合成企业环境，模拟真实组织架构、会议邮件与行业工作流，并自动化生成经质量校验的评估查询。平台全程不使用客户数据，内置隐私与内容安全筛查，将评估数据集创建从数天手工流程转为可复现自动化，节省约30万美元，并成为Copilot首个标准化评估基线。

title: Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences
summary: OpenAI will honor a shared robots.txt signal to help website operators communicate their AI training preferences to participating providers.
content: OpenAI will honor a shared robots.txt signal to help website operators communicate their AI training preferences to participating providers.

light_analysis.summary: OpenAI 宣布将遵循一项共享的 robots.txt 信号，网站运营者可以通过该文件向参与这一机制的 AI 服务商表达其内容是否可用于 AI 训练。此前网站方通常需要针对不同爬虫分别设置规则，缺少统一、机器可读的表达渠道。该举措让内容方在数据授权上拥有更明确、成本更低的表达方式，也为 AI 训练数据的获取提供了行业层面的自律参考。其实际效果取决于其他 AI 服务商的加入程度与执行情况。

title: Community safety report and new protections for teens
summary: OpenAI is strengthening violence prevention in ChatGPT with expanded safeguards, earlier interventions, and a new commitment to public safety reporting.
content: OpenAI is strengthening violence prevention in ChatGPT with expanded safeguards, earlier interventions, and a new commitment to public safety reporting.

light_analysis.summary: OpenAI 发布社区安全报告，宣布加强 ChatGPT 的暴力预防机制，通过扩展安全防护措施、提前介入潜在风险内容，并首次承诺定期向公众披露安全报告。同时，该举措还包含面向青少年用户的新保护措施，旨在降低未成年人接触有害内容的风险。此举反映出监管压力与社会舆论下，AI 公司正从被动响应转向主动治理，安全能力与透明度逐渐成为大模型产品的核心竞争力之一。对行业而言，这也可能推动更多厂商建立类似的安全报告与青少年保护标准。

title: Credit Saison achieves 954% ROI in a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot
summary: Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.
content: Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.

light_analysis.summary: 日本金融公司 Credit Saison（信贷赛尚）公布了其 ChatGPT Enterprise 试点项目的成果：实现 954% 的投资回报率（ROI）。该试点由公司管理层与员工共同参与推进，在验证了效率与收益后，公司将这一试点成果转化为全公司范围的正式部署。这条信息来自 OpenAI 官方发布的客户案例，核心信息在于企业级大模型应用的量化回报：接近 10 倍的 ROI 为 ChatGPT Enterprise 的商业价值提供了一个可供参考的标杆，也有助于说服更多金融等传统行业客户从试点走向规模化落地。不过，该案例原文未披露 ROI 的具体测算口径、试点覆盖人数、使用场景以及成本结构，因此该数字的适用范围仍需谨慎看待。
